newsitem.title: USA: Surge in sterling, U.S. stocks and bonds boosts dollar.
newsitem.headline: Surge in sterling, U.S. stocks and bonds boosts dollar.

text.p: A surging British pound pulled the dollar higher against other major currencies Friday while solid economic data spurred rallies in both stocks and bonds, further bolstering the dollar, foreign exchange dealers said.

Optimism over increased unity within Britain's ruling Conservative party and fresh data supporting higher British interest rates sent the pound to a 20-month high against the German mark and 3-1/2 year high against the Japanese yen.
The buying of pounds at the expense of European currencies and yen aided the dollar against those currencies, dealers said.
The dollar was pummelled below the 111.00 yen level overnight in Tokyo but revived after Japanese buyers came to the rescue. It ended at 111.65 yen, up from Thursday's close of 111.28.
Against the mark, the dollar steadily marched higher to close at 1.5305 marks, compared with 1.5283 at Thursday's close.
"The move in sterling did prompt a buy-dollar attitude. That action aside, I think dollar/yen is very bullish and will head higher," said Doug Lee, dealer at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.
The dollar also strengthened due to sharp gains in U.S. financial markets after data on September wholesale prices and retail sales showed slow, steady growth with modest inflation.
Retail sales rose a surprising 0.7 percent in September, fuelled by strong auto sales, but revised August data showed a 0.2 percent drop after an original 0.2 percent gain.
The Producer Price Index remained relatively tame, rising 0.2 percent overall, and 0.3 percent excluding food and energy.

Stocks rallied on the news, with the Dow Jones industrial average rising more than 50 points in early trading. The Dow was up 36 points in late afternoon trading at 5,957. The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond climbed half a point, underpinning the dollar, dealers said.

"The data were noninflationary and that made it look good for the dollar overall. We're not going to see a big sell-off in the equity and bond markets," said Tim Summerfield, senior dealer at Bank of Boston.

The gains in sterling reflected a strong end to the ruling Conservatives' party conference. A speech by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke seemed to mend rifts within Prime Minister John Major's party, analysts said.

Conference pledges included a 20 percent basic tax rate for all and a reduction and eventual abolition of capital gains and inheritance taxes. However, despite Major's strong unity message, analysts said it was unclear how long the bullish sentiment would last.

The pound also responded positively to an article in the London newspaper The Times, which predicted a rise in sterling, as well as to an encouraging retail sales survey from the Confederation of British Industry that hinted at steady British economic growth.

"The U.K. has one of the strongest economies in Europe and there's a chance we might have an interest rate increase there. They are also not frightened of having a stronger currency," said Summerfield.

U.S. trade dwindled in the afternoon as other markets closed early ahead of Monday's Columbus Day holiday. While the U.S. foreign exchange market will officially be open on Monday, volume is expected to be light as dealing rooms will be thinly staffed, traders said.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2535 Swiss francs from 1.2495 at Thursday's close. The dollar edged up to Canadian $1.3512 from $1.3511.
